> Verify that application documentation states the expected security features
that browsers using the application must support (such as HTTPS, HTTP
Strict Transport Security (HSTS), Content Security Policy (CSP), and other
relevant HTTP security mechanisms). It must also define how the
application must behave when some of these features are not available (such
as warning the user or blocking access).

I think this requirement is mixing client and server responsibilities. How are HTTPS, HSTS, and CSP considered browser features? These are server-side / deployment-side configuration items. Also, how are HSTS and CSP expected to be detected or handled at the application level?

Is it really a good idea to block a user because their browser doesn’t fully support a specific CSP level? What exact business logic is a developer needs to write, and how would the application detect this?

“**browsers using the application**” is clumsy; It's good to write “browsers used to access the application”.

comments.body:
> I think this requirement is mixing client and server responsibilities.

It lists browser features, as the requirement states.

> How are HTTPS, HSTS, and CSP considered browser features? These are server-side / deployment-side configuration items.

HSTS, CSP - with a server-side HTTP response header field, the server introduces a command to the browser. So it **is** a browser feature.

> Also, how are HSTS and CSP expected to be detected or handled at the application level?

It can be achieved by analyzing browser-supported features via caniuse.com and making a decision based on "the oldest version of that browser we can support".

> Is it really a good idea to block a user because their browser doesn’t fully support a specific CSP level? 

Does the requirement ask to block the user? (No, it does not == please read the requirement). It asks you to decide it based on your application needs.

> What exact business logic is a developer needs to write, and how would the application detect this?

This question probably should be rephrased. In general, ASVS does not dictate how to implement solutions.

My concern is more about how this requirement is framed for ASVS readers, who are typically thinking in terms of server configuration + documentation, not browser internals.

caniuse.com example is good for a design-time decision about a minimum browser baseline. The current wording reads like a runtime decision for each request.

> Does the requirement ask to block the user?

the requirement does not mandate blocking, it only gives blocking as an example.

Offtopic: Based on what information comes the statement how typical ASVS reader is thinking?

> caniuse.com example is good for a design-time decision about a minimum browser baseline. The current wording reads like a runtime decision for each request.

Runtime decision for each request can be made based on minimum browser baseline information that is analyzed before. 3.1.1 requirement is for that analysis to be done and documented. 3.7.5 is to apply this in practice (runtime).

| # | Description | Level |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| **3.1.1** | Verify that application documentation states the expected security features that browsers using the application must support (such as HTTPS, HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), Content Security Policy (CSP), and other relevant HTTP security mechanisms). It must also define how the application must behave when some of these features are not available (such as warning the user or blocking access). | 3 |
| **3.7.5** | Verify that the application behaves as documented (such as warning the user or blocking access) if the browser used to access the application does not support the expected security features. | 3 |
Thanks, @elarlang, for the information. I am closing this ticket, as there is a good chance my interpretation of the requirement differs from others.
